You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.

- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.

- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. - observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). - move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

# Block-building task notes (UR5e + parallel gripper, box parts)

## Core mechanics
- move_part(part,x,y,z): picks part, places center at (x,y,z), arm returns home. Returns ok + final_pose.
- Positions are part CENTERS. Upright parts: table-resting z = size_z/2. Stacked: bottom = top of support.
- get_task gives part sizes + 3 orthographic images (top x/y, front x/z, side y/z). Target coords NOT given — infer from images using metric grids + part sizes for exactness.

## CRITICAL LESSONS
1. **NEVER make parallel (multiple) move_part calls in one block.** A parallel move caused a part to fall over (upright=false) and left the arm stuck mid-grasp (gripper closed, not at home). Always one move at a time.
2. **`planning_cpu_budget` failures are TRANSIENT** — just retry the same move. Often succeeds on 2nd/3rd try. Long parts time out more often; interleave with other parts and retry.
3. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on an already-placed/stuck part** = it's on its side or blocked; the gripper can't grab non-upright parts. Hard to recover without reset_scene (which resets everything).
4. **`recovery_state_not_safe`** = the move disturbed something (a part fell). Observe immediately.
5. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on the part you're moving** can also mean the planner can't find a path. Retry or change approach.
6. Once you place a part, it's HARD to move again (planner may refuse if it's buried). Build order matters: put base + supports first, stack on top. A buried part is a trap.
7. Planner slows dramatically as scene clutters (wall_s grew from 16s to 700s+ per move). Budget is consumed fast. Keep moves efficient.

## Strategy that works
- Read 3 views, build a self-consistent (x,y,z) per part: z from stacking chain, x from top/front, y from top/side.
- Build bottom-up: base slab first, then supports on it, then stacks. Vertical cube chains are easy & reliable (small parts, clear support).
- Verify each part's bottom overlaps its support's top in x AND y before relying on it.
- The planner's support check is a good feedback signal: if it rejects with a support reason, your z or support assumption is wrong.

## Reading orthographic views
- Top view: horizontal=x, vertical=y (looking down -z).
- Front view: horizontal=x, vertical=z (looking +y).
- Side view: horizontal=y, vertical=z (looking -x).
- Overlapping/occluded parts are the hard part. Distinguish front-vs-back in y from side view, and near-vs-far in x from front view.
- Exact positions: touching parts share edge or centerline; use sizes to snap to multiples of 0.005.

## This run's result
Could not fully complete a 31-part structure: coordinate inference from views was too uncertain for the dense middle, a part (3) fell and got stuck, planner flakiness ate budget. Placed base + right tower correctly. Partial score.

messages.content:
You control a UR5e robot arm with a parallel gripper in a physics simulator. Your job is to build a target structure out of box-shaped parts that start parked on the table.

Units and frame: all positions are part centers in meters, in the world frame; z is up and the table surface is z = 0. Every part stays upright, so only its center position matters (yaw 0).

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

# Block-building task notes (UR5e + parallel gripper, box parts)

## Core mechanics
- move_part(part,x,y,z): picks part, places center at (x,y,z), arm returns home. Returns ok + final_pose.
- Positions are part CENTERS. Upright parts: table-resting z = size_z/2. Stacked: bottom = top of support.
- get_task gives part sizes + 3 orthographic images (top x/y, front x/z, side y/z). Target coords NOT given — infer from images using metric grids + part sizes for exactness.

## CRITICAL LESSONS
1. **NEVER make parallel (multiple) move_part calls in one block.** A parallel move caused a part to fall over (upright=false) and left the arm stuck mid-grasp (gripper closed, not at home). Always one move at a time.
2. **`planning_cpu_budget` failures are TRANSIENT** — just retry the same move. Often succeeds on 2nd/3rd try. Long parts time out more often; interleave with other parts and retry.
3. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on an already-placed/stuck part** = it's on its side or blocked; the gripper can't grab non-upright parts. Hard to recover without reset_scene (which resets everything).
4. **`recovery_state_not_safe`** = the move disturbed something (a part fell). Observe immediately.
5. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on the part you're moving** can also mean the planner can't find a path. Retry or change approach.
6. Once you place a part, it's HARD to move again (planner may refuse if it's buried). Build order matters: put base + supports first, stack on top. A buried part is a trap.
7. Planner slows dramatically as scene clutters (wall_s grew from 16s to 700s+ per move). Budget is consumed fast. Keep moves efficient.

## Strategy that works
- Read 3 views, build a self-consistent (x,y,z) per part: z from stacking chain, x from top/front, y from top/side.
- Build bottom-up: base slab first, then supports on it, then stacks. Vertical cube chains are easy & reliable (small parts, clear support).
- Verify each part's bottom overlaps its support's top in x AND y before relying on it.
- The planner's support check is a good feedback signal: if it rejects with a support reason, your z or support assumption is wrong.

## Reading orthographic views
- Top view: horizontal=x, vertical=y (looking down -z).
- Front view: horizontal=x, vertical=z (looking +y).
- Side view: horizontal=y, vertical=z (looking -x).
- Overlapping/occluded parts are the hard part. Distinguish front-vs-back in y from side view, and near-vs-far in x from front view.
- Exact positions: touching parts share edge or centerline; use sizes to snap to multiples of 0.005.

## This run's result
Could not fully complete a 31-part structure: coordinate inference from views was too uncertain for the dense middle, a part (3) fell and got stuck, planner flakiness ate budget. Placed base + right tower correctly. Partial score.

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

# Block-building task notes (UR5e + parallel gripper, box parts)

## Core mechanics
- move_part(part,x,y,z): picks part, places center at (x,y,z), arm returns home. Returns ok + final_pose.
- Positions are part CENTERS. Upright parts: table-resting z = size_z/2. Stacked: bottom = top of support.
- get_task gives part sizes + 3 orthographic images (top x/y, front x/z, side y/z). Target coords NOT given — infer from images using metric grids + part sizes for exactness.

## CRITICAL LESSONS
1. **NEVER make parallel (multiple) move_part calls in one block.** A parallel move caused a part to fall over (upright=false) and left the arm stuck mid-grasp (gripper closed, not at home). Always one move at a time.
2. **`planning_cpu_budget` failures are TRANSIENT** — just retry the same move. Often succeeds on 2nd/3rd try. Long parts time out more often; interleave with other parts and retry.
3. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on an already-placed/stuck part** = it's on its side or blocked; the gripper can't grab non-upright parts. Hard to recover without reset_scene (which resets everything).
4. **`recovery_state_not_safe`** = the move disturbed something (a part fell). Observe immediately.
5. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on the part you're moving** can also mean the planner can't find a path. Retry or change approach.
6. Once you place a part, it's HARD to move again (planner may refuse if it's buried). Build order matters: put base + supports first, stack on top. A buried part is a trap.
7. Planner slows dramatically as scene clutters (wall_s grew from 16s to 700s+ per move). Budget is consumed fast. Keep moves efficient.

## Strategy that works
- Read 3 views, build a self-consistent (x,y,z) per part: z from stacking chain, x from top/front, y from top/side.
- Build bottom-up: base slab first, then supports on it, then stacks. Vertical cube chains are easy & reliable (small parts, clear support).
- Verify each part's bottom overlaps its support's top in x AND y before relying on it.
- The planner's support check is a good feedback signal: if it rejects with a support reason, your z or support assumption is wrong.

## Reading orthographic views
- Top view: horizontal=x, vertical=y (looking down -z).
- Front view: horizontal=x, vertical=z (looking +y).
- Side view: horizontal=y, vertical=z (looking -x).
- Overlapping/occluded parts are the hard part. Distinguish front-vs-back in y from side view, and near-vs-far in x from front view.
- Exact positions: touching parts share edge or centerline; use sizes to snap to multiples of 0.005.

## This run's result
Could not fully complete a 31-part structure: coordinate inference from views was too uncertain for the dense middle, a part (3) fell and got stuck, planner flakiness ate budget. Placed base + right tower correctly. Partial score.

The target is given only as images. You are not told the target position of any part; you must infer it.

Tools:
- get_task(): the list of parts (index, size_m [x, y, z]) and images of the finished target structure. The images are orthographic views: a top view (looking down -z, horizontal axis x, vertical axis y), a front view (looking along +y, horizontal axis x, vertical axis z) and a side view (looking along -x, horizontal axis y, vertical axis z). Each view has a metric grid with labeled coordinates in meters, and each part is labeled with its index. The robot arm is not part of the target.
- observe(): the current position of every part, whether it is upright, and the arm/gripper state.
- move_part(part, x, y, z, yaw_deg=0): picks up one part and places it with its center at (x, y, z), then returns the arm home. The planner rejects moves it cannot do safely (no collision-free path, no support under the destination, etc.) and reports why. A failed or bad move can disturb other parts, so observe() after anything unexpected.
- reset_scene(): puts every part back at its parked start. Use it if the scene is ruined. It does not refund the budget.
- run_python(code): runs Python in a scratch directory that contains task.json (part sizes only), state.json and your memory/ folder. Use it for geometry and bookkeeping. It cannot touch the simulator or see the images.
- list_memory(), read_memory(path), write_memory(path, content): a persistent memory/ folder that survives across tasks.
- submit(): ends the episode and scores it. The episode passes only if every part is within 5 mm of its target position, upright, resting on what it should rest on, and the whole structure stays still for one second.

Reading positions off the grid is only approximate. Use the part sizes to make positions exact: a part resting on the table has z = size_z / 2, a part resting on others has its bottom at the top of its supports, and parts that touch in the images usually share an exact edge or center line.

Physics matters: a part can only be placed where something (the table or parts already placed) will support it, and parts placed too early can block later moves. Decide the build order yourself.

At the start of each task, read your memory. Before you submit, write down anything that would help you on future tasks: what worked, what failed and why, and reusable code. Keep notes short and general, not specific to this task's coordinates. The episode also ends if you run out of turns, tokens or time, in which case the current scene is scored as is.

# Block-building task notes (UR5e + parallel gripper, box parts)

## Core mechanics
- move_part(part,x,y,z): picks part, places center at (x,y,z), arm returns home. Returns ok + final_pose.
- Positions are part CENTERS. Upright parts: table-resting z = size_z/2. Stacked: bottom = top of support.
- get_task gives part sizes + 3 orthographic images (top x/y, front x/z, side y/z). Target coords NOT given — infer from images using metric grids + part sizes for exactness.

## CRITICAL LESSONS
1. **NEVER make parallel (multiple) move_part calls in one block.** A parallel move caused a part to fall over (upright=false) and left the arm stuck mid-grasp (gripper closed, not at home). Always one move at a time.
2. **`planning_cpu_budget` failures are TRANSIENT** — just retry the same move. Often succeeds on 2nd/3rd try. Long parts time out more often; interleave with other parts and retry.
3. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on an already-placed/stuck part** = it's on its side or blocked; the gripper can't grab non-upright parts. Hard to recover without reset_scene (which resets everything).
4. **`recovery_state_not_safe`** = the move disturbed something (a part fell). Observe immediately.
5. **`no_feasible_removal_or_grasp` on the part you're moving** can also mean the planner can't find a path. Retry or change approach.
6. Once you place a part, it's HARD to move again (planner may refuse if it's buried). Build order matters: put base + supports first, stack on top. A buried part is a trap.
7. Planner slows dramatically as scene clutters (wall_s grew from 16s to 700s+ per move). Budget is consumed fast. Keep moves efficient.

## Strategy that works
- Read 3 views, build a self-consistent (x,y,z) per part: z from stacking chain, x from top/front, y from top/side.
- Build bottom-up: base slab first, then supports on it, then stacks. Vertical cube chains are easy & reliable (small parts, clear support).
- Verify each part's bottom overlaps its support's top in x AND y before relying on it.
- The planner's support check is a good feedback signal: if it rejects with a support reason, your z or support assumption is wrong.

## Reading orthographic views
- Top view: horizontal=x, vertical=y (looking down -z).
- Front view: horizontal=x, vertical=z (looking +y).
- Side view: horizontal=y, vertical=z (looking -x).
- Overlapping/occluded parts are the hard part. Distinguish front-vs-back in y from side view, and near-vs-far in x from front view.
- Exact positions: touching parts share edge or centerline; use sizes to snap to multiples of 0.005.

## This run's result
Could not fully complete a 31-part structure: coordinate inference from views was too uncertain for the dense middle, a part (3) fell and got stuck, planner flakiness ate budget. Placed base + right tower correctly. Partial score.
